To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the SARS coronavirus requires the lysosomal cysteine protease catheptin L for its entry into host cells.
cathepsins L and B are required for SARS coronavirus entry, but that cathepsine B is not sufficient for entry, and that the proteases are activated by a low pH environment in the endosome.

SARS-CoVs are sensitive to lysosmotropic agents, which block infection by preventing the fusion of virus and cell membranes, but that protease treatment of the viruses can reverse the effect of these drugs, suggesting that the virus requires a protease to fuse with cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the cellular receptors and the cellular entry pathway of SARS-CoV.
the molecular mechanism of SARS-CoV cell entry.
the development of novel antiviral strategies against emerging infectious diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SARS-CoVs enter cells by a unique, three-stage process that is dependent on the S protein and the endosomal protease, cathepsin-L.
the proteolytic processing of SARS-CoV spike glycoprotein in the endosome is a key step in the entry process and is mediated by a lysosomal cysteine protease catheptin L.
SARS-CoVs enter the cells via a pH-independent pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have discovered an inhibitor of SARS-CoV that is a protease inhibitor of cathepsins L.
SARS-CoVs infect cells by binding to a receptor, followed by endocytosis, and proteolytic cleavage of SARS-CoV Spike (S) glycopeptide by cathepsins.

the SARS-CoV spike protein is a unique fusion protein that is activated through proteolytic cleavage by cathepsins L and B, and that the activation of the spike protein is a key determinant in the viral life cycle and a potential target for therapeutic intervention.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a new class of inhibitor for the SARS-CoV, which is a virus that causes a severe respiratory infection.
the cathepsin inhibitors we identified can be used to prevent the entry of SARS-CoV into host cells.
cathepsins L are involved in the infection process of SARS-CoV, and the inhibition of cathepsins may be a potential therapeutic strategy for the treatment of SARS.
